title: Sourdough Starter Kit
subtitle: Your 4-day plan to a bubbly, active sourdough starter from scratch.
intro: Starting a sourdough starter is simpler than you think. All you need is flour, water, a jar, and a little patience. In 4 days you'll have a living culture ready to bake with. This guide gives you everything you need — no experience required.
supplies: Unbleached all-purpose flour or bread flour
Whole wheat or rye flour (for the initial feedings — adds wild yeast)
A kitchen scale (grams are much easier than cups)
A rubber band or tape to mark the level
A loose lid, cloth, or coffee filter + rubber band

days.title: Day 1: Mix & Wait
days.summary: Combine flour and water to create your starter's first home.
steps: In your jar, mix 50g whole wheat flour + 50g all-purpose flour + 100g water.
Stir vigorously for about 60 seconds to incorporate air.
Mark the level on the jar with a rubber band.
Cover loosely (not airtight — it needs to breathe).
Place in a warm spot (75–80°F is ideal). Top of the fridge or near the oven works.
days.whatToExpect: Not much will happen today. The mixture will look like thick pancake batter. That's perfect.

days.title: Day 2: First Feeding
days.summary: Discard and feed to start building the yeast population.
steps: You may see a few small bubbles — that's bacteria starting to wake up!
Discard about half of the mixture (you should have ~100g remaining).
Add 50g all-purpose flour + 50g water. Stir well.
Mark the new level and cover loosely.
days.whatToExpect: You might notice a slightly sour or yeasty smell. Some bubbles appearing. This is normal! The starter may also look completely inactive — also normal.

days.title: Day 3: Building Momentum
days.summary: Continue feeding. You should see more activity now.
steps: Discard all but about 75g of starter.
Feed with 50g all-purpose flour + 50g water. Stir well.
Mark the level, cover, and return to the warm spot.
Start checking every few hours — you want to see it rise and fall.
days.whatToExpect: More bubbles! The starter should be noticeably rising between feedings. It may double in size, which is a great sign. The smell might be a bit funky — like overripe fruit or vinegar. This is normal and will mellow out.

days.title: Day 4: The Float Test
days.summary: Test if your starter is ready to bake with!
steps: Feed your starter as usual: discard to 75g, add 50g flour + 50g water.
Wait 4–6 hours until it has doubled and is very bubbly.
Do the float test: drop a small spoonful into a glass of water.
If it floats — congratulations, your starter is active and ready to bake!
If it sinks — no worries. Keep feeding once or twice a day for 2–3 more days.
days.whatToExpect: A healthy starter should reliably double in size within 4–8 hours of feeding. It will smell pleasantly sour, like yogurt or mild vinegar. It will be full of bubbles and have a slightly domed top at peak activity.

faqs.question: My starter isn't bubbling at all after 2 days. Should I start over?
faqs.answer: No! Some starters are slow to get going, especially in cool kitchens. Move it to a warmer spot (aim for 78°F) and keep feeding. It can take up to 7 days in some cases.

faqs.question: There's dark liquid on top of my starter. Is it ruined?
faqs.answer: That's called 'hooch' — it's alcohol produced by hungry yeast. It means your starter needs to be fed. Just pour it off (or stir it in for a more sour flavor) and feed as usual.

faqs.question: Can I use only all-purpose flour?
faqs.answer: Yes, but whole wheat or rye in the first couple of feedings helps introduce more wild yeast and gets things going faster. After that, all-purpose is perfectly fine.

faqs.question: What do I do with all the discard?
faqs.answer: Don't throw it away! Use it to make crackers, pancakes, waffles, pizza dough, or banana bread. Check our Recipes page for ideas.

faqs.question: How do I store my starter long-term?
faqs.answer: Once established, you can keep it in the fridge and feed it once a week. Take it out the night before you want to bake, give it 2 feedings at room temperature, and it'll be ready to go.

faqs.question: My starter smells like nail polish remover. Is that bad?
faqs.answer: Not ruined! That acetone smell means it's very hungry and producing acetic acid. Feed it more frequently (twice a day) and it will balance out.

faqs.question: What kind of water should I use?
faqs.answer: Filtered or bottled water is best. If your tap water is chlorinated, let it sit out uncovered for an hour before using, or use a basic carbon filter. Chloramine (used in some cities) won't evaporate — use filtered water in that case.

faqs.question: Can I speed this up?
faqs.answer: Warmth is your best friend. Keep it at 78–82°F for faster fermentation. Using some rye flour in your feedings can also help. But honestly, patience is part of the process!
